title: What TOK Examiners Look for in an Exhibition
summary: Learn what TOK examiners look for in an exhibition: specific objects, real-world context, prompt links, evidence, and convincing justification.
body_markdown:
If you are trying to understand what **TOK examiners look for in an exhibition** , focus on four priorities: **specific real-world objects, explicit links to the chosen IA prompt, convincing justification, and appropriate evidence** . Examiners do not primarily reward unusual objects, sophisticated vocabulary, attractive displays, or lengthy philosophical discussion.


Strictly speaking, your teacher marks the exhibition and the IB externally moderates a sample. Nevertheless, your submitted commentary must communicate its reasoning to an unfamiliar reader who cannot ask what an object means or why you selected it.


### What the TOK exhibition officially requires


According to the[IB overview of Theory of Knowledge](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/) , TOK is assessed through an exhibition and a **1,600-word essay** . The exhibition is the internal assessment component and contributes **33% of the final TOK result** .


You must:


- Select **one of the 35 prescribed IA prompts** without changing its wording.
- Choose **three specific objects** , or images of objects, connected to that prompt.
- Identify each object's **real-world context** .
- Submit a combined commentary of no more than **950 words** .
- Explain each object-prompt link and justify each object's contribution.
- Provide appropriate citations and image references.


The submitted file is assessed, not the visual sophistication of a classroom display. Presentation cannot compensate for weak analysis in the commentary.


### The four main examiner priorities


The exhibition is assessed **holistically out of 10** . The central issue is how successfully it demonstrates the manifestation of TOK in the world around us.


Examiner priority Strong work Weak work


Objects and contexts Identifies particular objects in meaningful situations Uses generic categories such as “a phone”


Prompt links Explains how object details illuminate the exact prompt States that an object “relates” without showing how


Justification Shows why each object adds a distinct insight Explains only why the topic is interesting


Evidence Supports claims with object features and contextual facts Makes unsupported generalizations about knowledge


The[TOK exhibition rubric guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-rubric-how-to-score-top-marks) and[RevisionDojo TOK Exhibition Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader/rubric/tok-exhibition) can help you apply these priorities during revision.


### Specific objects need real-world context


A strong object is not simply a type of thing. “A scientific article” is generic; a named article your Biology class used to compare conflicting treatment claims is specific. Similarly, a particular photograph taken at a documented event has more analytical value than an unidentified image found online.


Context does not require a complete history. Include details affecting the object's significance as evidence, such as **who produced it, when and where it appeared, how it was used, who trusted it, and what purpose it served** .


Personal objects can be effective because their provenance is clear, but personal importance is not automatically a TOK argument. An inherited recipe becomes useful when it reveals something about embodied knowledge, cultural transmission, authority, or the limits of written instructions. The[guide to selecting TOK exhibition objects](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/selecting-the-right-objects-for-your-tok-exhibition) offers further tests for specificity and analytical potential.


### Prompt links must explain a knowledge process


A weak commentary might state, “This object connects to the prompt because evidence is important.” That sentence announces a connection but does not explain the knowledge process visible in the object.


A stronger version would say: “This laboratory record suggests that evidence becomes adequate only after a community applies agreed methods, because my class repeated the procedure before accepting the result.” This identifies what happened, explains the standard used to judge evidence, and draws a qualified conclusion.


Use the prompt's central terms throughout your analysis. This keeps the commentary focused on knowledge rather than drifting into a description of the object's general subject.


### Justify why each particular object belongs


Explanation establishes a connection. **Justification** shows why this specific object deserves a place and what it contributes that the other two do not.


Ask three questions for every selection:


1. What does this object reveal that my other objects do not?
2. Which feature or contextual fact supports that insight?
3. Could any generic example replace it without weakening the argument?


For a prompt about experts, one object might demonstrate how specialist methods create authority. Another could examine how institutions communicate expertise, while a third could show how conflicts of interest weaken trust. This creates range without producing three unrelated discussions.


The[TOK exhibition commentary guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-create-an-engaging-tok-exhibition-commentary) explains how to assign each object a separate analytical role.


### Evidence should support the analysis


TOK evidence is not limited to academic quotations. It can include wording printed on an object, a design feature, its documented use, the method through which it was produced, or a relevant personal encounter.


For example, if the object is a correction notice attached to a news article, the changed wording, publication date, original claim, and editorial policy can support an argument about reliability. Simply declaring that “the media can be biased” cannot.


Cite factual context, online information, statistics, and images appropriately. References establish credibility, but they do not replace your explanation of why the evidence matters for the prompt.


### A practical structure for each object


Each object section should normally do the following:


- **Identify and contextualize** the exact object.
- Make a clear **prompt-linked claim** .
- Analyse a knowledge issue such as reliability, interpretation, authority, perspective, values, or power.
- Use a concrete object feature or contextual fact as evidence.
- Justify the object's distinct contribution.
- Qualify the claim when a limitation or alternative interpretation improves it.


A counterclaim is not a separate compulsory element of the assessment instrument. Include one only when it sharpens the analysis rather than as a formulaic addition.


### Common mistakes that lower marks


The most damaging mistakes concern reasoning rather than presentation:


- Choosing generic images without identifiable provenance.
- Describing an object's history instead of analysing it.
- Treating the prescribed prompt as a broad theme.
- Claiming a link without explaining how it works.
- Selecting three objects that repeat the same conclusion.
- Using TOK terminology without applying it accurately.
- Assuming personal importance provides sufficient justification.
- Spending too many words on a general introduction.
- Exceeding the **950-word maximum** .


Study[TOK exhibition examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/tok-exhibition) to identify effective analytical moves, not to copy objects or wording.


### A September-to-November preparation plan


Schools set their own internal deadlines, so confirm yours with your teacher. In September, review the[TOK exhibition prompt guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-prompts-b4a14cd7) , test several objects, and establish their contexts.


In October, write one central claim for each object before drafting. Approximately **250-300 words per object** is a useful planning range, although equal sections are not an official requirement.


In November, check that every object is identifiable, every claim has support, and each object contributes something different. Then verify citations, image labels, prompt wording, and word count using the[step-by-step TOK exhibition checklist](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-excel-in-your-ib-tok-exhibition-complete-step-by-step-guide) .


### Conclusion


TOK examiners and moderators want a convincing demonstration of **TOK in the real world** . Strong exhibitions connect three specific, contextualized objects to one prescribed prompt through visible evidence and distinct justification.


RevisionDojo's prompt guides, exemplars, and TOK Exhibition Grader can help you test those elements. The final selection and commentary, however, must remain your own carefully reasoned work.
